How Can We, as ‘Ulama, Expect Such Respect and Reverence from Ordinary People? — Can We Earn Respect by Disgracing ‘Ilm (Islamic Knowledge)?

The ‘Ulama undoubtedly deserve respect and honour. From an Islamic perspective, ‘Ilm (Islamic knowledge) and those who possess it hold a special status. At the same time, recognizing and valuing knowledgeable and wise individuals is essential to the intellectual development, moral refinement, and overall well-being of any society. Therefore, it is not unreasonable for the ‘Ulama to expect society to hold them in esteem and show them due respect.

But the question is:

Do we really possess any distinctive qualities that justify our expectation of such respect and honour from society?

Do we consider ourselves entitled to this respect merely because of our religious identity, titles, or outward appearance?

Is simply identifying oneself as one of the ‘Ulama sufficient to earn the respect, trust, and affection of society?

If we entertain the notion that the mere identity of being an ‘Alim is enough to guarantee special respect, then we are undoubtedly engaging in self-deception.

In reality, the honour of ‘Ilm becomes meaningful in a person's life only when it brings about positive changes in their thinking, character, and conduct. If ‘Ilm fails to cultivate in us truthfulness, steadfastness in upholding the truth (*al-Haqq*), a spirit of sacrifice, justice, moral integrity, self-respect, and God-consciousness (*Taqwa*); if it fails to contribute to our spiritual refinement, courtesy, and cultured conduct, then the social and moral significance of that knowledge becomes questionable.

This is particularly true when a scholar's conduct reveals undue flattery and sycophancy in pursuit of the favour of those in power and influence, compromises with principles for personal gain, or shifts in position in the hope of securing privileges and material benefits. Such behaviour creates a clear disconnect between the dignity of the knowledge that a scholar possesses and the personal standing that he demonstrates through his conduct.

Here, we need to ask ourselves a fundamental question:

If we sacrifice our self-respect and commitment to principles in order to gain the favour of those in power and influence, then what moral justification do we have for expecting special respect from ordinary people?

We expect society to honour ‘Ilm, yet we ourselves often undermine its dignity through our own conduct. This is not merely a matter of individual weakness; its adverse effects sometimes extend to the public image of the ‘Ulama community as a whole.

Even more concerning is that, in certain instances, our conversations, mutual conduct, ways of expressing differences of opinion, and exchanges on social media fall short of the standards of courtesy and refinement expected of us. We sometimes engage in *Ghibah* (backbiting), disparagement, slander, and the use of vulgar and indecent language against one another. Instead of expressing disagreements through reasoned arguments and dignified discourse, we resort to personal attacks, ridicule, and verbal abuse.

Yet ordinary people expect more from an ‘Alim than merely religious knowledge. They also expect to see that knowledge reflected in his conduct, personality, moral integrity, and way of life. People do not simply wish to hear the teachings of ‘Ilm from an ‘Alim; they also want to see those teachings embodied in his life.

Dress and outward identity may distinguish someone as an ‘Alim, but it is character and conduct that truly make him worthy of respect. Institutional rank and outward recognition may confer a degree of formal prestige, at least temporarily, but genuine respect is earned through knowledge, character, moral integrity, personality, and conduct.

When these qualities are lacking, even the identity of being an ‘Alim cannot guarantee the respect one expects. On the contrary, an individual's conduct and attitude may damage the collective image of the entire ‘Ulama community.

Therefore, the primary responsibility for safeguarding the honour and dignity of the ‘Ulama community rests with the ‘Ulama themselves. We cannot afford to complacently blame ordinary people, social changes, or the realities of the times for the erosion of our standing.

We must also critically examine our own conduct, moral positions, allegiance to centres of power, tendency towards compromising principles, and the nature of our mutual relationships. In many instances, we ourselves are more responsible for losing public respect than others are. Before expecting respect from others, we must first cultivate ourselves in such a way that our ‘Ilm, righteous deeds (*‘Amal*), character, and personality naturally make us worthy of that respect.

In this connection, a statement by the renowned worshipper and ascetic, Fudayl ibn ‘Iyad (Rahimahullah, 105–187 AH), is particularly noteworthy. His words highlight, in a profoundly meaningful manner, the self-respect that the ‘Ulama should uphold, the importance of preserving the dignity of ‘Ilm, and the consequences of exploiting religious knowledge for worldly interests.

He said:

“If the ‘Ulama themselves had preserved their own dignity, demonstrated deep commitment and devotion to the Din, safeguarded the honour of ‘Ilm, and employed it in the manner and for the purposes prescribed by Allah, even the necks of the most powerful and mighty would have bowed before them. People would have obeyed them and become their devoted followers. Moreover, the Din and the Millah would have grown stronger.

But, regrettably, they themselves failed to preserve their dignity. So long as their worldly interests remain unaffected, they give little thought to the harm being done to the Din. Instead, they have used their knowledge indiscriminately to serve the interests of those attached to worldly pursuits, merely to secure for themselves the privileges and benefits allotted to them with ease.

As a consequence, they themselves have become humiliated and disgraced in the eyes of people. *Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji‘un!* What a grave calamity!”
